name: Plant
review: Located in a modest standalone building on busy Merrimon Avenue just north of downtown, Plant has regularly topped lists of the nation’s best vegan restaurants since it opened in 2011. It’s 90% organic and mostly gluten-free, but the bold and artful flavor profiles executive chef Jason Sellers coaxes from his ingredients lack nothing. The popular lasagna cruda and housemade vegan cheese plate are menu anchors, with other items rotating depending on the season and Sellers’s inspiration. Customers should save room to finish the meal with a scoop (or two) of the chef’s impossibly creamy and decadent dairy-free ice creams.

name: Tall John’s
review: When chef Trevor Payne opened Tall John’s in 2022, his goal was to create a cozy neighborhood tavern where guests could drop in to relax with the simple pleasures of an ice-cold martini and perfectly roasted chicken. Nestled in an art-filled, historic wooden building at the edge of North Asheville’s tree-lined, residential Montford neighborhood, Payne’s restaurant delivers all that and more. In addition to the martinis and chicken, the menu of satisfying American-European classics feels like a warm hug with straightforward but beautifully executed options like pillowy Parker House rolls, grilled quail, and a quintessential Caesar salad.

name: Rosetta's Kitchen & The Buchi Bar
review: Relocated in 2022 to a space just down the street from the funky Lexington Avenue building it had inhabited for 20 years, Rosetta’s still maintains its mellow, hippie vibe and serves the same menu of simple, fresh, affordably priced vegan and vegetarian soul food. The veggie burger and peanut butter-baked tofu are legendary, but the Buddha Bowl is another good choice with its simultaneously healthy and indulgent tumble of rice, smoky tofu, avocado, greens, and more (add the house-cultured kimchi for a kick). The spacious patio area offers on-tap, locally made Buchi kombucha plus cocktails, mocktails, and housemade sodas.

name: Luminosa
review: Everything about the experience at Luminosa is a treat, from the comfortable elegance of the wood-and-brass-filled dining room in the historic downtown Flat Iron Building to the friendly service and beautifully prepared Italian fare. But it’s the restaurant’s impeccable sense of place, staunch commitment to local sourcing, and zero-waste practices that earned it a 2025 Michelin Green Star, along with a Bib Gourmand designation for delivering outstanding fare at an excellent value. The bone marrow “tator tots” with horseradish aioli are a reliable place to start. From there, a wood-fired pizza might be in order — play it safe with a classic margherita or explore a bit with toppings such as lemon, fennel, and smoked mozzarella. The housemade pastas and meat dishes are also foolproof. Still, those in the know will also grab something from the contorni menu, which showcases vegetables sourced fresh from Western North Carolina farms.

name: The Market Place
review: Chef William Dissen’s the Market Place celebrated its 45th anniversary in 2024 with a semifinalist nod for the James Beard Outstanding Restaurant award. Opened in 1979, and in its current Wall Street location under Dissen’s ownership since 2009, the Market Place is Asheville’s landmark farm-to-table restaurant and a cornerstone of the city’s food scene history. Sampling the house pickles, fresh vegetable small plates, and charcuterie is a must. The seasonally rotating menu also showcases fresh local meats and trout, as well as Carolina seafood options. The Benton’s bacon Old Fashioned with maple syrup is a classic complement to the meal.

name: Cúrate
review: When chef Katie Button opened Cúrate in 2011, she set a high bar for Asheville’s then-nascent restaurant scene. With a 2022 James Beard Award for Outstanding Hospitality under its belt, the Spanish tapas concept still charms adoring crowds in its friendly, yet refined, historic downtown space with shareable classics like jamon Iberico, Galician-style octopus, and goat cheese-stuffed piquillo peppers. The bar stocks an impressive list of Spanish and Basque vermouths, sherries, and wines.

name: Chai Pani
review: After winning the 2022 James Beard Award for Outstanding Restaurant, chef Meherwan Irani’s lighthearted homage to Indian street food outgrew the tiny downtown space where it earned its reputation, and in 2024, moved to much larger digs on the South Slope. The massive dining room welcomes guests withan explosion of Chai Pani’s signature buoyantly colorful decor and joyful Bollywood verve. Selections like the popular kale pakoras and lime-kissed matchstick okra fries share the menu with thali plates, grilled kebabs, pav street sandwiches, and Indian truck stop-style small plates such as the crispy sabudana vada tots. Chai Pani doesn’t take reservations, but on weekends, diners can wait for their table at the upstairs cocktail and pani puri bar.

name: Good Hot Fish
review: Operating from a tiny, hip counter-service space on the bustling South Slope, chef Ashleigh Shanti’s Good Hot Fish restaurant definitely isn’t your grandma’s fish camp. But it does deliver — on brightly colored plastic Frisbees, no less — a craveable, high-end yet decidedly unfancy take on Southern fish camp cuisine. The namesake sandwich of perfectly fried North Carolina catfish and buttermilk tartar sauce layered unceremoniously between two pieces of white bread sounds far too simple for its price tag. But the first steaming, melt-in-your-mouth bite has the power to instantly mint new believers. The Ranchovy bowl (an expertly gussied-up version of the classic iceberg lettuce salad) is another good bet, as are many other sides, including the deeply satisfying Sea Island red peas and rich, gooey baked macaroni.

name: Gypsy Queen Cuisine
review: Before opening her cozy West Asheville brick-and-mortar restaurant a decade ago, Lebanon native Suzy Phillips earned a diehard following dishing out her mother’s recipes from a food truck. With her little cafe, Phillips provides a friendly, welcoming mix of bohemian Asheville and the Middle East, with comfy, colorful pillows, pictures of her mom, and casual, clean-up-after-yourself counter service. The menu has something for everyone, from garlicky, lemony Lebanese fries to labneh, fattoush, spice-rich m’dardara, and lamb kafta. Sandwich seekers can fill fresh pitas with chicken, beef, or lamb shawarma, as well as housemade vegan seitan, falafel, and Lebanese-spiced beets. Deli cases and shelves near the entrance offer baklava and other tempting dessert options, plus Middle Eastern foods to take home.

name: Leo's House of Thirst
review: An outstanding wine selection, well-crafted seasonal food menu, and welcoming rustic outdoor space have helped make this second Haywood Road offering from the Admiral owner, Drew Wallace, a favorite neighborhood gathering spot. Popular dishes include deviled eggs with smoked honey and bacon or chicken liver mousse with blackberry jam and fennel pollen. Also, chef Austin Inselmann’s housemade pastas never disappoint. Brunch is served until 4 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays, while Monday evenings feature a special menu of Italian fare, with antipasti, spaghetti and meatballs, linguine and clams, and gelato for dessert.

name: Potential New Boyfriend
review: There’s no other place in Asheville quite like Potential New Boyfriend. A chic jewel box of bright colors; luxurious, mismatched furniture; and vivid artwork with an eclectic vinyl collection and top-notch sound system, PNB has established itself as the West Asheville neighborhood’s hip, home-away-from-home hangout. For savory snacking, there’s everything from grilled cheese sandwiches to savory aperitivo, like marinated olives and labneh with crudité. But it’s best not to sleep on the housemade ice creams and mindblowing desserts from pastry chef Dana Amromin — highlights include coconut tres leches and apricot cardamom Turkish Delight sundae. Owner Disco has crafted an impressive yet approachable selection of outside-the-box wines, amaros, vermouths, and wine-based cocktails. Helpful staff are always happy to help with suggestions and guidance.

name: Sunny Point Café
review: A West Asheville comfort food institution, Sunny Point serves breakfast all day along with lunch and dinner options, sourcing seasonal ingredients from its on-site production garden. It’s worth the unavoidable wait on weekend mornings for a crack at the sausage and cheese-stuffed French toast, carrot hotcakes, or locally lauded shrimp and grits. Dishes can be paired with anything from espresso to sweet tea to cocktails. Guests can wait for their table next door in the restaurant’s Rabbit Hole bakery and coffee shop before dining indoors or on the covered patio near the restaurant’s expansive, flower-filled garden.

name: OWL Bakery
review: Asheville is blessed with many excellent bakeries, but Old World Levain (OWL) is in a class by itself. Founder Susannah Gebhart learned the art and science of crafting her naturally leavened old-world breads and European pastries from a fourth-generation Spanish-Italian baker. Her bakeshop in West Asheville and the newer second location on Charlotte Street near downtown are often crowded with locals lined up for the perfect, airy baguettes and Instagramable sourdough loaves, as well as shatter-in-your-mouth croissants, jewel-like tarts sparkling with crystallized herbs, sugared Scandinavian cardamom buns, and other pastry delights. A sizable menu of coffee drinks and teas helps wash it all down. The Charlotte Street location recently expanded to include a dedicated retail cake shop.

name: Neng Jr.'s
review: Dip down a West Asheville side street and enter through the back door to discover the warm and utterly unique dining experience that chef-owner Silver Iocovozzi brings to life in a colorful, 17-seat space at Neng Jr.’s. Drawing inspiration from his Filipino roots, the chef delivers a rotating parade of vibrant offerings such as adobo oyster accented with cured quail egg yolk and the subtle, saline pop of sea grapes, crab fried rice, sinigang smoked wings, and a sculpted longanisa sausage pithivier. The cheese ice cream is a dessert favorite. The friendly staff carefully explains each dish to guests, so there’s no need to Google unfamiliar items.

name: Jargon
review: Terrific cocktails and consistently delicious modern American fare may be what lure folks to Jargon, but once inside, the compact space itself becomes a key part of the experience. Owners Shelly and Sean Piper have won awards for their respectful and beautiful renovation of the historic building, and Shelly pours her art history background into the decor, which includes fascinating collections of whimsical artwork, curios, and antiques. A cool way to kick off a Jargon meal is with its signature Ice Breaker cocktail — an Old Fashioned served inside a smoked ice sphere. Bread service with housemade potato rolls and black shallot butter, and the pumpkin coconut soup make good entry points for mains that often include choices such as roasted duck breast, local chicken leg confit, and whole mountain trout.

name: Corner Kitchen
review: Located not far from the gates of the Biltmore Estate, Corner Kitchen is a cornerstone of Asheville’s modern restaurant industry. Its cozy, two-story pebbledash building was constructed in 1895, one of the original Biltmore Village structures. Since it opened in 2004, it’s cemented a reputation for delivering consistently excellent, straightforward fare to both locals and tourists — including famous visitors, like Barack and Michelle Obama in 2010. After the building was ravaged by severe flooding from Tropical Storm Helene in 2024, owners Kevin Westmoreland and Joe Scully completely rebuilt it, reopening in August 2025 to help lead the charge for Biltmore Village’s recovery. CK’s corn and crab chowder and the pecan-crusted trout are Asheville institutions, and on weekends, folks line up out the door to fill up on favorites like biscuits and gravy, boozy French toast, and pimento cheese tots.

name: Taqueria Muñoz
review: With its flagship location in an unassuming West Asheville strip mall space and newer second shop just south of Biltmore Village, Taqueria Muñoz is regarded as a local culinary treasure for its lush and flavorful sopes, tortas, tacos, burritos, tamales, and more. The dominant language is Spanish, the dining experience is no-frills, the portions are hearty, and the prices are pleasantly affordable. Most dishes feature choices of pork pastor, carnitas, steak asada, chicharron, cabeza, and tongue, but vegetarians don’t have to settle for rice and beans — additional options include spinach and mushrooms, huitlacoche, nopales, and squash blossoms. Drink options include a rotating selection of housemade aguas frescas.

name: Posana
review: Chef Peter Pollay’s elegant Posana restaurant has anchored the heart of downtown with its Pack Square location for more than 15 years, priding itself on a vast, award-winning wine list and luxurious, seasonally rotating cocktail menu. Many are shocked to learn after sampling the stellar housemade breads and pastas, that the restaurant is 100% gluten-free — the concept was inspired by Pollay’s wife, Martha, who has celiac disease. Menu exploration can begin with trusted favorites — the sesame seed breadsticks and lemony kale salad with local manchego. Entree options typically include the unfailingly delectable wine-braised short ribs as well as pastas and local chicken and pork dishes. Posana’s new South Asheville location offers the same menu and a similarly plush, upscale vibe with the welcome addition of an outdoor dining space.
